newsitem.title: USA: Dlr/yen ends off in US, hurt by intervention fears.
newsitem.headline: Dlr/yen ends off in US, hurt by intervention fears.

text.p: The dollar ended little changed against the yen, trimming losses on fears of central bank intervention fueled by remarks from a senior Japanese financial official and the U.S. trade representative, experts said.
"It is quite clear that both the U.S. and Japanese goverments want the dollar not to go up further," said Takanobu Igarashi, senior economist at Sanwa Bank Ltd in New York.
"We don't expect intervention is coming at around this level," he said when the dollar was trading near 125.60 yen.
Sakakibara, director-general of the Ministry's International Finance Bureau, was speaking to currency dealers in Tokyo.
While U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsy did not directly address the exchange rate, her remarks were also seen as weighing on the dollar.

After a speech during an Economic Strategy Institute conference in Washington D.C. on Wednesday, Barshefsky told reporters that the United States is concerned about its trade imbalance with Japan. She stressed that Washington does not wish to see the trade gap grow wider.

The Japanese government will release its customs-cleared merchandise trade surplus for March overnight, while the Commerce Department puts out the U.S. international trade figures for February on Thursday at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.
Economists polled by Reuters predicted, on average, the U.S. trade gap shrank to $10.1 billion in February from $12.71 billion in January.
Nervousness about the possibility of central bank intervention also prompted traders to close out short yen positions against a broad array of currencies.

"People are buying back yen that they previously sold against the European complex, including the mark, Swiss franc and British pound, and also against the dollar," said Marc Chandler, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
In late trading, the mark traded around 72.78/81 yen, down from 72.92/95 yen in very early dealings.

John Hazelton, chief foreign exchange dealer at Manufacturers and Traders Bank, said: "I think the major motivation behind people buying the yen is fear of the Japanese and U.S. authorities coming in and intervening, selling dollars and buying yen."
